title: How BASE Jumping Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain BASE jumping, an acronym for jumps from buildings, antennas, spans, and earth (cliffs). They cover its history from early stunts by Frederick Rodman Law, to Carl Boenish's filming of El Capitan jumps in 1978 (Sunshine Superman) and his acronym-based numbering system, the gear differences between skydiving and BASE (ram air canopies, sliders, larger pilot chutes, static lines, off-heading openings, tracking), the legal issues and trespassing, National Park Service rules, the safety advice from Tom Aulo, wingsuit flying and deaths in the sport. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about New Zealand's Mongrel Mob and a note about Disney-themed gangs.
topics: National Park Service BASE jumping ban

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts chat about music of the seventies (Earth Wind and Fire, the Commodores), the blues, and movies, then set up the episode topic of BASE jumping.

segments.title: What BASE jumping is
segments.summary: BASE is an acronym for buildings, antennas, spans, and earth (cliffs). The hosts discuss the legal and practical issues with each category, and the risks of jumping from antennas and bridges, including the Idaho bridge where jumping is legal year round and a recent fatality.

segments.title: Danger and early history
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the risks of BASE jumping and the advice that injuries are nearly certain. They trace early stunts by Frederick Rodman Lewis in the 1910s and the 1978 El Capitan jumps by Carl Boenish, documented in Sunshine Superman. They describe early El Capitan jumpers Brian Schubert and Michael Pelkey, who were slammed into the cliff.

segments.title: BASE numbering and naming
segments.summary: Boenish is credited as the father of BASE jumping. The hosts explain the numbering system for completing all four BASE categories, the early name 'best' that was rearranged to 'BASE', and Phil Smith as BASE number one.

segments.title: BASE gear: ram air parachutes and deployment
segments.summary: Ram air canopies replaced round parachutes. Because BASE jumpers have less time than skydivers, they need sliders and larger pilot chutes for faster deployment. Static lines are used for very low jumps, and the hosts explain the dangers of slamming into structures and off-heading openings.

segments.title: Body position, tracking, and mental preparation
segments.summary: Tracking, a bullet-like body position, reduces the chance of an off-heading opening. Tom Aulo's criteria for suitability include quick reactions, organization, and attention to detail.

segments.title: Legality, National Park Service, and guarding spots
segments.summary: BASE jumping is largely illegal, involving trespassing and deceiving guards. The National Park Service restricted it, the old parachute law originally aimed at hunters, and fines and confiscation for offenders. Jumpers keep spot locations secret, and a local-only code is enforced.

segments.title: Skydiving, tandem jumps, and movies
segments.summary: The hosts compare skydiving training with BASE jumping, discuss a video of a woman forced out of a tandem jump, and briefly digress on movie remakes and the Ghostbusters reboot.

segments.title: BASE deaths, wingsuits, and safety advice
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the death toll in BASE jumping, Dean Potter's death at Yosemite, wingsuit flying and its origins with Patrick de Gayardon and John Carter, and Tom Aulo's advice on getting started, including writing sealed letters and taking a manufacturer class.

segments.title: Listener mail: Mongrel Mob and Disney gangs
segments.summary: A listener writes about New Zealand's Mongrel Mob, and the hosts mention a tweet about Disney-themed gangs.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listeners to get in touch and sign off.
